newsitem.title: UK: French poll talk fuels attack of market EMU nerves.
newsitem.headline: French poll talk fuels attack of market EMU nerves.

text.p: Mounting speculation of a snap French election dragged down the franc and its European fellows against the mark on Monday as it fanned a fresh outbreak of market nerves over economic and monetary union.
The prospect of an early French poll sparked fears power could pass to a Socialist-led alliance which might struggle to reconcile pro-EMU policies with efforts to boost growth.
The market was already jittery ahead of the European Commission's 1997-98 economic forecasts due on Wednesday and amid doubts over Italy's proposed mini-budget, analysts said.

"The big theme this week is renewed doubts about the EMU project," said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ International in London. "This (French election speculation) has just thrown another uncertainty into the pot."

A lower house budget commission on Friday rejected Italy's proposed 15.5 trillion lire mini-budget -- designed to help Italy catch the first wave of EMU in 1999 -- and made it likely a confidence vote would be needed to force the measure through.
On Saturday, however, Italian news agency ANSA reported that the International Monetary Fund had criticised the planned mini-budget for stressing EMU at the expense of structural reform.

What should have been a week of good news for Italy, with preliminary April CPI data expected to show healthy inflation rates and open the door to a rate cut, had been darkened by the budgetary uncertainty, analysts said.
"The beneficial edge has been taken off that good news story," said Hannah.
The lira fell to a low of 993.50 per mark in early Europe from Friday's European close of 988.40/90, though it had recovered to 991.60/992.10 by 0909 GMT.
The French franc was quoted at 3.3730/35 to the mark, down from late Friday's level of 3.3694/99.
As talk swirled of an early election in May or June, French President Jacques Chirac's office said he would broadcast to the nation at 1800 GMT on Monday.
Earlier, Chirac set in motion the procedure for dissolving the National Assembly by holding statutory consultations with Prime Minister Alain Juppe and parliamentary leaders.
An opinion poll published on Monday suggested the ruling centre-right coalition, which controls 478 of the Assembly's 577 seats, would lose up to 150 but retain an overall majority.
While that should be positive in EMU terms, analysts warned the election campaigning could be negative for the franc.

"Any election campaign would present an opportunity for the letting of much malcontent with France's economic performance and possibly anti-EMU noises," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
As for the left, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin on Sunday said he would not, if elected, introduce further EMU-targeted austerity measures if that meant even longer jobless queues.

"A snap election would increase the risk of an EMU delay, because if the Socialists win then fiscal consolidation would become more difficult," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN AMRO here.
The Socialists also favoured allowing Italy into the first round of EMU, which Germany strongly opposed, he added.
Speculation was rife last week that France and Germany were cooking up a deal to exclude Italy and Spain from the single currency launch -- though Bonn and Paris hotly denied that.
An EU source told Reuters on Friday that the European Commission would this week predict Italy would miss the 3.0-percent deficit-to-GDP target for monetary union in 1997.
But the Commission's forecasts would indicate Germany and France meeting the three percent goal, Britain's Observer newspaper reported on Sunday.
